title: Jamais je ne t'oublierai

description.main: A 2019 artist's book by French-Moroccan photographer Carolle Bénitah (1965-2024), reworking anonymous flea-market photographs with gold leaf into a meditation on inherited memory and its gaps. Winner of the 2020 Prix HiP for photography monograph.
description.extended:
Jamais je ne t'oublierai is a 2019 artist's book by the French-Moroccan photographer Carolle Bénitah (1965–2024), in which anonymous flea-market photographs are reworked with gold leaf into a meditation on inherited memory and its gaps.

Published by L'Artiere Edizioni, curated by Laura Serani and designed by Teresa Piardi, the 56-page volume replaces Bénitah's own family archive — subject of her earlier book Photos Souvenirs — with photographs of strangers bought at flea markets. Faces are partly obscured under applied gold leaf, a surface that both erases and reflects, multiplying the identities of people whose names are lost. Bound in Japanese spiral stitching, it appeared in an edition of 1,000 and won the 2020 Prix HiP photography award.

Born in Casablanca in 1965, Bénitah trained at the École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne and spent ten years as a fashion designer before turning to photography in 2001, graduating with distinction from the École Nationale Supérieure de la Photographie in Arles. Represented by Galerie Clémentine de la Féronnière, she used embroidery, beading, and gold leaf on found and family photographs to work through memory and loss. She died in Marseille in 2024.
description.artist_bio: Carolle Bénitah (1965-2024) was a French-Moroccan photographer born in Casablanca. She trained as a fashion designer at the École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne before turning to photography in 2001, later graduating with distinction from the École Nationale Supérieure de la Photographie in Arles (2015). Her practice, rooted in the intimate, addressed family, desire, loss, and mourning through interventions — embroidery, beading, gold leaf — on found and personal photographs. Represented by Galerie Clémentine de la Féronnière in Paris, she died in Marseille in 2024.
